A1.justification: Both PDFs describe JudgeLM. All 30 pages of v1 and 40 pages of v2, including tables, figures, equations and appendices, support comparison. Retained material can be matched despite relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original JudgeLM benchmark evaluations, scaling experiments, component ablations, efficiency measurements and qualitative judging examples.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds original benchmark evaluations, controlled comparisons, robustness analyses and human-agreement measurements.

M1.justification: The proposed score-first judging procedure, optional explanations, swap augmentation, reference support and reference drop are retained. Alternative backbones and explanation-first output are evaluated as experimental variants, without replacing the proposed method.

E1.justification: v2 adds ToxicChat toxicity evaluation, RewardBench evaluation and a scenario with reference answers embedded in distracting paragraphs. The original JudgeLM and PandaLM coverage remains. MM-Vet was already present in v1; v2 adds quantitative human-annotated evaluation within that existing multimodal coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Auto-J-13B, InstructScore-7B and vanilla Vicuna-13B, whose output failures are reported in the text. Additional comparisons introduce OpenAI Moderation and reward-model families including Prometheus, UltraRM, TIGERScore, Tulu-2-DPO and Qwen1.5. GPT-4 also becomes a direct comparator in new consistency and multimodal evaluations.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include serial-versus-parallel efficiency controls, explanation-first judging, alternative-backbone and matched-LLaMA component experiments, three-level human MM-Vet annotations, reference paragraphs of 50–400 words, and pairwise-versus-multiple ranking metrics. RewardBench uses four subsets and an aggregate score. The original training split and core fine-tuning settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained scaling and three-component ablations, v2 adds output-order and backbone analyses, dataset/component controls, category breakdowns, reference-noise sensitivity and multiple-answer consistency tests. Appendix A.4 adds teacher-reliability comparisons and a 500-case examination of GPT-4 wins to investigate possible favoritism.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new human-agreement measurements and sampled answer-quality audit add evaluation evidence, without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Existing result entries in Tables 1–6 are retained, but many results are added. Examples include 91.74% human agreement on MM-Vet, 89.66% ToxicChat accuracy and a 78.5 RewardBench score (Tables 13, 14 and 17). Table 3 adds 400-minute and 24-minute serial JudgeLM measurements. The earlier $60 versus $0.50 evaluation-cost estimate is removed.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly specifies the swap-outcome cases defining first- and second-position bias and formally defines their normalized counts and absolute difference in Equations 5–7. This is limited formalization of previously reported custom statistics. The standard classification formulas are explanatory additions; no theorems or proofs are introduced.

C1.justification: The dataset, scalable judging, benchmark leadership, efficiency and over-90% agreement claims remain substantially unchanged. The revised conclusion makes a limited novelty distinction: analyzing two biases while introducing a new format bias, rather than simply claiming analysis of three biases.

C2.justification: v2 refines format bias from fixed-template overfitting to dependence on internal versus reference knowledge, distinguishing it from multiple-answer formats. New discussions interpret specialist-versus-teacher performance, mathematical weaknesses, reference-noise degradation, GPT-4 answer preference and teacher biases. Applicability discussions now address stronger backbones and the mismatch between training queries and real-world usage.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly documents automated filtering, independent author reannotation and cross-validation, metric calculations, and academic-only dataset usage. Table 11 adds the GPT API version. These substantially expand documentation without establishing that the original experiments were rerun. Core hyperparameters and the code/model link remain; some earlier timing-accounting and annotation details are omitted.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through Auto-J, InstructScore, UltraFeedback, Prometheus, reward-model research and knowledge distillation. Appendices A.1 and A.4 add dataset comparisons and detailed distinctions from PandaLM. Section 2.2 replaces the earlier criticism of PandaLM's model-size limitation with emphasis on unaddressed biases.

P1.justification: The abstract and main seven-section progression remain largely intact. v2 edits wording and headings, rewrites selected bias and efficiency explanations, and relocates the existing extension discussion into Appendix A.3 with new section pointers. Author information, conference headers and acknowledgments are also updated; much of the expansion is new scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial comparative and diagnostic table displays, expands and subdivides Table 1, and adds a multi-turn example as Figure 20. Existing Figures 3–4 and 17–18 are consolidated onto shared pages. The earlier multimodal examples remain, renumbered as Figures 21–24, rather than being replaced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's limited generalization evidence and mainly illustrative extension demonstrations through human-scored MM-Vet, ToxicChat, RewardBench and robustness evaluations. New efficiency and matched-backbone component controls better isolate the sources of reported benefits, while expanded dataset documentation improves transparency. Uncertainty estimates and some annotation details remain incomplete, but the added validation resolves important weaknesses in the empirical support.
